patterns.note: fetch only rejects on network failure, so you have to throw on a bad status yourself or a 500 is treated as success. Always set retries: the default of 10 with no maxTimeout runs for about 17 minutes.

patterns.title: Abort immediately on an error that will never succeed
patterns.note: AbortError skips onFailedAttempt, shouldRetry, and shouldConsumeRetry entirely and rejects at once. Pass an existing error to keep it as the cause: new AbortError(originalError).

patterns.title: Configure the backoff curve
patterns.note: randomize is off unless you set it, and without it every client that failed at the same instant retries at the same instant. maxTimeout is the ceiling per wait, not a total budget; use maxRetryTime for that.

patterns.title: Log or instrument each failure
patterns.note: attemptNumber starts at 1. If this callback throws, retrying stops and the promise rejects with your thrown error, not the original failure, so keep logging code inside a try or keep it trivial.

patterns.title: Decide per error whether to retry
patterns.note: shouldRetry runs after onFailedAttempt and never runs for AbortError or for a non-network TypeError, which is aborted regardless of what you return here.

patterns.title: Do not let 429 responses consume retries
patterns.note: A failure that does not consume a retry also does not advance the backoff, so the delay stays flat. Pair it with maxRetryTime or a server that keeps returning 429 will loop until the process ends.

patterns.title: Wait for the server's Retry-After header
patterns.note: onFailedAttempt may return a promise, and p-retry awaits it before its own backoff wait, so this adds to the delay rather than replacing it. There is no built-in Retry-After support.

patterns.title: Cancel retries from the outside
patterns.note: Aborting rejects with the reason you passed to abort(), and it interrupts the sleep between attempts, not just the gaps. The package deliberately does not install signal handlers itself.

patterns.title: Make a permanently retrying version of a function
patterns.note: makeRetriable keeps the original signature and types, so it is the cleanest way to retrofit retries onto an existing client without touching call sites. Arguments are re-evaluated per call, not per attempt.

patterns.title: Retry a function that takes arguments
patterns.note: p-retry passes the attempt number as the first argument to your function, so handing it a function that expects real parameters gives you getUser(1) on the first try. Wrap it in an arrow function.

patterns.title: Cap total retry time instead of attempt count
patterns.note: maxRetryTime is measured with performance.now(), so a clock change does not extend or shorten it. Combining infinite retries with a time budget is the pattern for startup checks such as waiting on a database.

patterns.title: Test retry logic without waiting
patterns.note: The delays come from the global setTimeout, so any fake timer library works. Without this a single test of a five-retry path can sit for half a minute of wall clock.

guide.whatIs: p-timeout takes a promise and gives you back a decorated promise that rejects with a TimeoutError if the original has not settled within a given number of milliseconds. You can swap the rejection for a fallback function, a custom error, or a plain resolve with undefined, and you can abort the wrapper early with an AbortSignal. It is about 700 bytes gzipped with zero dependencies. One thing it explicitly does not do: it never cancels the work you wrapped. The underlying promise keeps running, keeps holding memory, and keeps its side effects. p-timeout only stops you waiting for it. Its 45 million weekly downloads come almost entirely from being a transitive dependency of build tools and test runners rather than from people installing it directly.
useIf: You need a deadline on a promise from an API that accepts no AbortSignal, such as an older database driver, a callback wrapped with promisify, or a third-party SDK method
You want a fallback on timeout rather than a rejection: options.fallback runs your function (retry, cached value, degraded response) instead of throwing

You need the timer itself to be controllable, either cleared early with the returned promise's .clear() method or swapped out via customTimers so sinon.useFakeTimers() does not freeze your production timeout
You want a typed TimeoutError class you can instanceof against and subclass, instead of matching on error message strings
skipIf: The thing you are timing out already accepts an AbortSignal: fetch, node:fs/promises, undici, most modern SDKs. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) is built into Node 18+ and every current browser, needs no dependency, and actually tells the callee to stop working. The README says this too, in a note at the very top

You expected the timeout to cancel the operation. It does not. A wrapped 30 second database query still runs for 30 seconds and still commits whatever it was going to commit; you just stopped listening at 5 seconds
You are on CommonJS. Versions 5 and up are ESM only, so require('p-timeout') throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM outside of Node's newer require-of-ESM support, and v7 additionally demands Node 20 or newer
You are adding it to a codebase that already imports p-retry, p-queue or got: all of them have their own timeout options, and a second timeout layer on top mostly produces confusing double failures
You need this in a browser bundle where every dependency is audited. Writing Promise.race against a setTimeout is roughly six lines and removes a supply chain entry
guide.setupReality: npm install p-timeout, no peer dependencies, no build step, TypeScript types included. The friction is module format and timers. Since v5 the package is ESM only with an exports map, so CommonJS projects and older Jest setups need either transformIgnorePatterns tweaks or a dynamic import(); v7 also sets engines.node to >=20, which quietly breaks CI runners still on Node 18. If your test suite calls sinon.useFakeTimers() or jest.useFakeTimers(), the internal setTimeout gets frozen and your timeout never fires, so you have to capture the real timer functions before faking and pass them through options.customTimers. Finally, remember to call .clear() on the returned promise in long-lived processes, otherwise the pending timer keeps the event loop alive until it expires.

alternatives.name: abort-utils
alternatives.when: You want native AbortSignal semantics and need to merge a timeout signal with a user-triggered cancel button

alternatives.name: p-retry
alternatives.when: The real problem is a flaky operation that should be retried with backoff, not one that should fail after a fixed deadline

alternatives.name: promise-timeout
alternatives.when: You are stuck on CommonJS and cannot consume an ESM-only package

guide.verdict: Well built and tiny, but for most new code AbortSignal.timeout() does the same job with no dependency and actually stops the work. Reach for p-timeout when you are bounding a promise from an API that gives you no cancellation hook, and accept that the operation keeps running behind your back.

apiStability.why: The options object shape has been stable since v5 in 2022 and v7 changed only the Node floor. The catch is that major versions regularly bump engines and module format, so upgrading is more about your runtime than your call sites

docsQuality.why: A single README that documents every option with a runnable example, plus an unusually honest section telling you to consider AbortSignal.timeout() instead

maintenance.why: Zero open issues and zero open PRs, but the last release and last push were both October 2025. That is finished-software quiet rather than abandoned, though nobody should expect fast turnaround on a report

ecosystem.why: 45M weekly downloads and part of the widely used sindresorhus promise-fun family, but only 305 stars: the traffic is transitive, coming through other packages rather than direct adoption

patterns.title: Reject a promise after a deadline
patterns.note: slowOperation() keeps running after the rejection; p-timeout only stops your await, it does not cancel anything.

patterns.title: Tell a timeout apart from a real failure
patterns.note: Always branch on instanceof TimeoutError rather than the message string, which is user-configurable.

patterns.title: Set your own timeout message or error
patterns.note: Subclass TimeoutError rather than Error for custom types, so callers checking instanceof TimeoutError still match.

patterns.title: Resolve with undefined instead of throwing
patterns.note: message: false is the only way to get a non-throwing timeout; the value is always undefined, so you cannot distinguish it from a genuine undefined result.

patterns.title: Run a fallback when the deadline passes
patterns.note: fallback may return a value or a promise; if the fallback itself hangs it has no deadline of its own, so wrap it in another pTimeout when that matters.

patterns.title: Clear the timer so it stops holding the event loop open
patterns.note: A pending 60 second timer keeps a Node process alive even after the wrapped promise settles early; .clear() releases it.

patterns.title: Abort the wait early with an AbortSignal
patterns.note: The signal aborts your wait, not longTask(). To actually stop the work, the task has to accept the signal itself.

patterns.title: Turn the timeout off with a config value
patterns.snippet:
const timeoutMs = config.timeoutMs ?? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY;

await pTimeout(job(), {milliseconds: timeoutMs});
patterns.note: Passing Infinity means never time out, which is handy for a single code path that has to support an opt-out.

patterns.title: Survive fake timers in tests
patterns.note: Capture the real timer functions before installing fake timers, otherwise the internal setTimeout is frozen and the timeout never fires.

patterns.title: Skip the dependency when the callee accepts a signal
patterns.note: AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any are built into Node 20 and current browsers; the aborted call actually stops and frees its resources.

patterns.title: Import it from a CommonJS file
patterns.note: v5 and later are ESM only; dynamic import is the portable escape hatch when you cannot convert the file.

guide.whatIs: pandas is the standard Python library for working with tabular data. Its DataFrame and Series structures give you labeled rows and columns plus readers and writers for CSV, Excel, SQL, Parquet, JSON and HDF5. You use it to load, clean, reshape, join, group and aggregate data that fits in memory, and it sits underneath most of the Python data stack, from scikit-learn workflows to one-off analysis notebooks. Development started at the hedge fund AQR in 2008 and it is now a NumFOCUS-sponsored community project.
useIf: You do exploratory analysis or data cleaning on datasets that fit comfortably in RAM
You need glue between formats and systems: CSV or Excel in, Parquet or SQL out, DataFrames into scikit-learn or plotting libraries
You work with time series and want resampling, rolling windows and date arithmetic that already handle the edge cases
You want the API with the largest body of examples, courses and answers in data tooling
skipIf: Your data is bigger than memory or your groupbys and joins are slow: pandas is mostly single-threaded, and polars or duckdb run the same workloads several times faster on large tables

You are upgrading a legacy codebase casually: pandas 3.0 (January 2026) turned copy-on-write on permanently, made the dedicated string dtype the default and removed long-deprecated APIs, so old 1.x/2.x code and a decade of Stack Overflow answers no longer match current behavior
The job is simple record shaping in a service: the csv module and plain dicts are lighter and easier to reason about than the index/axis model
You want strict schemas and lazy, optimizable query plans; pandas executes eagerly and validates nothing unless you bolt on extra tools
guide.setupReality: pip install pandas just works; prebuilt wheels exist for every mainstream platform so there is no compiler step. The friction is elsewhere: pandas 3.0 requires Python 3.11+, and the optional engines are separate installs you discover via ImportError at runtime (pyarrow for Parquet, openpyxl for Excel, SQLAlchemy for SQL, matplotlib for .plot). Migrating to 3.0 needs a real deprecation pass: chained assignment silently stops writing under copy-on-write, and code that relied on object-dtype strings can behave differently under the new string dtype.

alternatives.name: polars
alternatives.when: You want multicore speed and lazy execution on large tables with a stricter, more consistent API

alternatives.name: duckdb
alternatives.when: You would rather write SQL over Parquet/CSV files and only surface results as DataFrames

alternatives.name: dask
alternatives.when: You need the pandas API but the data is bigger than one machine's memory

guide.verdict: Still the default for in-memory data work in Python, with unmatched documentation and ecosystem gravity, and the 3.0 defaults fix its oldest footguns. But for large data or performance-sensitive pipelines, start with polars or duckdb instead of trying to make pandas fast.

apiStability.why: Deprecation cycles are long and documented, but 3.0 removed accumulated APIs and flipped core defaults (copy-on-write, string dtype), so upgrading old code and trusting old tutorials both take work.

docsQuality.why: The user guide, API reference and migration notes on pandas.pydata.org are among the most complete in open source, and whatsnew entries document every behavior change.

maintenance.why: Pushed the day of this review, NumFOCUS-backed with community and new-contributor meetings, and 3.0 has already had five patch releases since January 2026.

ecosystem.why: The center of PyData: scikit-learn, plotting libraries, database drivers and file-format tools all speak DataFrame, and 180M+ weekly PyPI downloads reflect that.

patterns.title: Load a CSV with explicit types
patterns.snippet:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv(
    'sales.csv',
    dtype={'store_id': 'int32'},
    parse_dates=['sold_at'],
)
patterns.note: In pandas 3 text columns load as the dedicated str dtype, not object; code that checked dtype == object for strings needs updating.

patterns.title: Filter rows with boolean masks
patterns.snippet:
recent = df[df['sold_at'] >= '2026-01-01']
big = df[(df['amount'] > 100) & (df['region'] == 'EU')]
patterns.note: Combine conditions with & and | plus parentheses; Python's and/or raise ValueError on Series.

patterns.title: Write to a subset without the chained-assignment trap
patterns.snippet:
df.loc[df['amount'] < 0, 'amount'] = 0

# WRONG under copy-on-write (writes to a discarded copy):
# df[df['amount'] < 0]['amount'] = 0
patterns.note: Copy-on-write is always on in pandas 3, so chained assignment never updates the original; use one .loc call for the whole operation.

patterns.title: Group and aggregate with named columns
patterns.snippet:
summary = (
    df.groupby('region', as_index=False)
      .agg(total=('amount', 'sum'), orders=('order_id', 'nunique'))
)
patterns.note: Named aggregation keeps flat column names; without it multi-stat aggs produce a MultiIndex that surprises everyone downstream.

patterns.title: Join two DataFrames safely
patterns.snippet:
orders = pd.merge(
    orders, customers,
    on='customer_id', how='left',
    validate='many_to_one',
)
patterns.note: validate='many_to_one' raises immediately if the right side has duplicate keys, which otherwise silently multiplies your rows.

patterns.title: Handle missing data
patterns.snippet:
df['qty'] = df['qty'].fillna(0)
df = df.dropna(subset=['customer_id'])
patterns.note: pandas 3 no longer silently downcasts dtypes after fillna, and inplace-style idioms from old tutorials are gone; assign the result back.

patterns.title: Parse timestamps and bucket by period
patterns.snippet:
df['ts'] = pd.to_datetime(df['ts'], format='%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S', utc=True)
monthly = df.set_index('ts').resample('MS')['amount'].sum()
patterns.note: Pass format when you know it; inference on messy columns is slow and can misread day/month order.

patterns.title: Pivot long data into a wide table
patterns.snippet:
wide = df.pivot_table(
    index='region', columns='month',
    values='amount', aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0,
)
patterns.note: pivot_table aggregates duplicates; plain .pivot raises on duplicate index/column pairs, which is usually what tells you the data is not what you thought.

patterns.title: Store results as Parquet
patterns.snippet:
df.to_parquet('out/sales.parquet', index=False)
back = pd.read_parquet('out/sales.parquet')
patterns.note: Requires pyarrow installed separately; prefer Parquet over CSV for anything you plan to re-read, it keeps dtypes and is far smaller.

patterns.title: Prefer vectorized ops over apply
patterns.snippet:
import numpy as np

# slow: row-wise Python loop
# df['margin'] = df.apply(lambda r: r['rev'] - r['cost'], axis=1)

# fast: whole-column arithmetic
df['margin'] = df['rev'] - df['cost']
df['tier'] = np.where(df['margin'] > 100, 'high', 'low')
patterns.note: apply(axis=1) runs a Python function per row and is often 100x slower than column arithmetic; reach for it last.

patterns.title: Cut memory with categoricals
patterns.snippet:
df['region'] = df['region'].astype('category')
df.info(memory_usage='deep')
patterns.note: Big win only when the column has few unique values; comparisons and merges between category and str columns need matching categories.

guide.whatIs: Papa Parse turns CSV text into JavaScript arrays or objects and back again. You hand it a string, a File from an input element, a URL to download, or a Node readable stream, and it gives you rows plus a metadata object describing what it found. The parser follows RFC 4180, so quoted fields containing commas and embedded newlines come out correct, which is where most hand-rolled split(',') code falls apart. It has zero dependencies, weighs under 7 KB gzipped, can auto-detect the delimiter, can run in a Web Worker so a 200 MB file does not freeze the tab, and can stream row by row instead of building one enormous array in memory. Papa.unparse goes the other direction and writes CSV from your objects.
useIf: You accept CSV uploads in the browser and need to parse them client-side, with a progress indicator and no server round trip; this is the case Papa Parse was built for and nothing else does it as well
Your input is real-world messy CSV: quoted fields with commas and newlines inside them, unknown delimiter (comma, semicolon, tab, pipe), a BOM at the start, inconsistent line endings
The files are big enough that reading everything into memory is a problem, and you want a step or chunk callback that processes rows as they arrive, with pause, resume, and abort
You also need to generate CSV for download, and would rather use Papa.unparse than write your own quoting and escaping rules
skipIf: You are server-side only. In Node the worker, download, withCredentials, LocalChunkSize, and RemoteChunkSize options all do nothing, and in NODE_STREAM_INPUT mode step and complete are unavailable too. csv-parse and fast-csv are built for Node streams and give you a better API there

dynamicTyping will corrupt your data and you have not thought about it: it converts "007" to 7, turns long numeric IDs into floats that lose precision past 2^53, and reads "NA" or "null" as strings while turning "true" into a boolean. For anything financial or identity-related, leave it off and coerce fields deliberately
You want TypeScript types in the box. Papa Parse ships plain JavaScript; types live in the separate @types/papaparse package, so an npm install alone leaves you with an untyped import

You need promises. Every asynchronous path is callback-based (complete, error, step, chunk) with no promise or async iterator API, so it does not compose with async/await without you writing the wrapper

Your files reliably exceed what a browser tab can hold and you need real backpressure or column-typed output. At that point stream it to the server, or use a columnar reader; Papa Parse's worker mode reduces jank but still copies every row across the worker boundary
guide.setupReality: npm install papaparse is genuinely painless: no dependencies, no peer dependencies, no build step, and it works from a script tag or a bundler. Two things surprise people. First, types are not included, so TypeScript users need npm install --save-dev @types/papaparse as a second step. Second, the package is browser-first: the default export targets the browser build, and the Node behaviors are documented as a list of options that quietly stop working rather than as a separate Node API. Worker mode also has a quirk that bites bundler users, because Papa builds the worker from its own script URL, and some bundler configurations make that URL unreachable, in which case parsing silently falls back or fails depending on setup. Everything else is config-object tuning against a single long options table.

alternatives.name: csv-parse
alternatives.when: You are in Node and want a real stream transform with backpressure, sync and async iterator APIs, and a large set of RFC-edge-case options.

alternatives.name: fast-csv
alternatives.when: Node again, but you want parsing and formatting under one friendly API with per-row validation and transform hooks.

alternatives.name: d3-dsv
alternatives.when: You are parsing modest CSV or TSV in a browser data-visualization context and want a tiny, synchronous parser with a row conversion function.

guide.verdict: For CSV in a browser, Papa Parse is still the right answer: correct on quoting, tiny, dependency-free, and the only option with worker and streaming support that just works. On the server it is merely adequate, and csv-parse or fast-csv fit Node's stream model better.

apiStability.why: The v5 config object has been stable since 2018; new options get added, existing option names and callback signatures do not change, and code written years ago still runs on 5.5.4.

docsQuality.why: papaparse.com/docs is a complete single-page reference for every config key and result field, with a live demo you can throw a real file at. The weak spot is Node: its limitations are a couple of README paragraphs rather than a documented API of their own.

maintenance.why: 5.5.4 shipped in June 2026 and the repository was pushed in July 2026, so it is not abandoned, but 190 issues are open (225 counting PRs) and plenty of them are years old with no maintainer reply.

ecosystem.why: Roughly 14.3 million weekly downloads, zero dependencies, community TypeScript definitions in @types/papaparse, and it is the parser behind a large share of CSV import features in web apps.

patterns.title: Parse a CSV string into objects
patterns.note: Parsing a string is synchronous and returns the result directly. Values stay strings unless you turn on dynamicTyping. skipEmptyLines: 'greedy' also drops lines that contain only delimiters and whitespace.

patterns.title: Parse a file chosen in the browser
patterns.note: Passing a File makes parsing asynchronous, so the return value is useless and you must use the complete callback. Add encoding: 'ISO-8859-1' when users upload files exported from older spreadsheet tools.

patterns.title: Fetch and parse a CSV by URL
patterns.note: download: true only works in the browser and is subject to CORS like any other request. In Node it is ignored, so fetch the body yourself and pass the string or stream.

patterns.title: Handle rows as they arrive instead of all at once
patterns.note: With step, results.data holds one row instead of the whole file, so memory stays flat. The parser argument gives you pause(), resume(), and abort(); pause and resume are what you need when your per-row work is asynchronous.

patterns.title: Process large files in batches
patterns.note: chunk gives you an array of rows per callback rather than one row, which is much faster than step for bulk inserts. Pause before an async call or Papa keeps feeding you chunks while your writes queue up.

patterns.title: Parse off the main thread
patterns.note: Worker mode is browser only and costs a serialization hop per row, so it is slower in total but keeps the page responsive. Functions in your config cannot cross into the worker, which rules out transform and beforeFirstChunk here.

patterns.title: Pipe a Node readable stream through Papa
patterns.note: In NODE_STREAM_INPUT mode the step and complete callbacks are unavailable; you listen for 'data' and 'end' events instead. worker, download, and the chunk-size settings do nothing in Node either.

patterns.title: Write CSV from objects
patterns.note: unparse quotes and escapes for you, which is the whole reason to use it. It builds the entire string in memory, so for very large exports write rows yourself in a loop or stream from the server.

patterns.title: Clean up headers and values while parsing
patterns.note: Doing typed conversion in transform is safer than dynamicTyping because you decide field by field. transformHeader also receives the column index as a second argument, useful when duplicate header names need disambiguating.

patterns.title: Check what went wrong and what was detected
patterns.note: Papa almost never throws; it collects problems in errors and keeps going, so an empty data array with a populated errors array is the failure mode to check for. TooFewFields and TooManyFields are the two codes you will see most.

patterns.title: Control delimiter detection and peek at the first rows
patterns.note: Auto-detection samples the beginning of the file, so a file whose first rows happen to contain semicolons inside quoted commas can be guessed wrong. Setting delimiter explicitly is both faster and safer when you control the source.

patterns.title: Wrap parsing in a promise
patterns.note: There is no built-in promise API, so most codebases end up with a helper like this. Do not use it together with step, because step-based parsing resolves with an empty data array.

guide.whatIs: Paramiko is a Python implementation of the SSHv2 protocol, giving you both a client and a server in pure Python instead of shelling out to the ssh binary. You get SSHClient for running remote commands, an SFTP client for file transfer, Transport and Channel for raw port forwarding and tunnels, and key classes for RSA, ECDSA and Ed25519. The cryptographic work is delegated to the cryptography package, so it is only pure-Python in the protocol sense. The maintainers say plainly in the README that most people running remote commands or copying files should use Fabric, which wraps Paramiko, and that direct Paramiko use is for people who need low-level primitives or an in-process sshd.
useIf: You need SSH from inside a Python process where subprocess-ing to the ssh binary is not acceptable: containers without an ssh client, Windows hosts, or sandboxes that block process spawning
You need to speak SFTP programmatically with stat, chmod, rename, and streaming file handles rather than driving sftp or scp as a child process
You need to write an SSH server in Python: Paramiko is one of the very few libraries that implements the server side of SSHv2 including auth callbacks and channel handling
You need low-level control over channels, direct-tcpip tunnels, agent forwarding, or per-connection algorithm negotiation via disabled_algorithms
skipIf: You just want to run a remote command or copy a file: Fabric is written by the same maintainer, sits on top of Paramiko, and handles connection reuse, sudo, and config parsing that you would otherwise write yourself

You need speed on large transfers: Paramiko does its framing and buffering in Python, and SFTP throughput is well below OpenSSH's scp or rsync on the same link, which is a recurring theme in the issue tracker
You need asyncio: the API is blocking and thread-based, so every call ties up a thread; asyncssh is the native async alternative

You need SSH features Paramiko does not implement: GSSAPI/Kerberos was removed entirely in 5.0.0, DSA keys were removed in 4.0.0, and SHA-1 based key exchange and RSA signatures are gone as of 5.0.0, so old appliances and legacy jump hosts can simply fail to connect
You want a quiet dependency: it pulls in cryptography, bcrypt, pynacl, and invoke, and 890 open issues sit against a project that releases a few times a year
guide.setupReality: pip install paramiko is usually fine because cryptography, bcrypt, and pynacl all ship wheels for common platforms, but on musl images or odd architectures you are compiling Rust and C, and that is where CI breaks. Since 4.0.0 invoke is a hard dependency rather than an extra, so the install is heavier than people expect. The real friction is behavioral: SSHClient rejects unknown host keys by default, so first-run scripts fail until you call load_system_host_keys() or set a policy; the widely copy-pasted AutoAddPolicy silently disables host key checking. Upgrading from 3.x to 5.x can break connections to older servers because SHA-1 kex, SHA-1 RSA signatures, DSA keys, and GSSAPI have all been removed.

alternatives.name: fabric
alternatives.when: You want the high-level command runner and file transfer API; same maintainer, built directly on Paramiko

alternatives.name: asyncssh
alternatives.when: Your app is asyncio-based and you want SSH client and server without dedicating a thread per connection

alternatives.name: scp
alternatives.when: You already have a Paramiko transport and only need scp-style file copying, which is faster than SFTP for bulk pushes

guide.verdict: Paramiko is still the reference SSH implementation for Python and the only realistic choice if you need the server side or raw channels. For ordinary remote commands and file copies, take the maintainers' own advice and use Fabric instead.

apiStability.why: The core SSHClient and SFTP surfaces have barely changed in a decade, but 4.0.0 and 5.0.0 removed DSA, GSSAPI, SHA-1 kex, and SHA-1 RSA signatures, and renamed PKey.from_path's passphrase argument to password, so recent majors break real deployments even when your code compiles.

docsQuality.why: docs.paramiko.org has full versioned API reference and an honest changelog that flags each backwards-incompatible removal with a warning box, but there are few end-to-end guides and common tasks like proxy jumps or keepalives are folk knowledge in issues and blog posts.

maintenance.why: Effectively one primary maintainer with a slow but real release cadence: 4.0.0 in August 2025, 5.0.0 in May 2026, last push May 2026. 890 open issues (1,188 including PRs) is a large backlog for a library this widely deployed.

ecosystem.why: The default SSH layer for Python: Fabric, Ansible's paramiko connection plugin, netmiko, and most network automation tooling sit on top of it, and it is imported by build and deploy systems everywhere.

patterns.title: Connect and run a command
patterns.snippet:
import paramiko

client = paramiko.SSHClient()
client.load_system_host_keys()  # trust ~/.ssh/known_hosts
client.connect("host.example.com", username="deploy", timeout=10)

stdin, stdout, stderr = client.exec_command("uname -a")
print(stdout.read().decode())
client.close()
patterns.note: Without load_system_host_keys() or an explicit policy, connect() raises SSHException on any host it has never seen. That is the correct default, not a bug.

patterns.title: Get the exit code and stderr of a command
patterns.snippet:
stdin, stdout, stderr = client.exec_command("exit 3; echo nope")

out = stdout.read().decode()
err = stderr.read().decode()
code = stdout.channel.recv_exit_status()  # read streams FIRST

if code != 0:
    raise RuntimeError(f"remote failed ({code}): {err}")
patterns.note: recv_exit_status() blocks until the command finishes. Call it before draining stdout and a command that writes more than the channel window (about 2 MB) deadlocks forever.

patterns.title: Authenticate with a private key file
patterns.snippet:
from paramiko import PKey, SSHClient

key = PKey.from_path("/home/me/.ssh/id_ed25519", password="passphrase-or-None")

client = SSHClient()
client.load_system_host_keys()
client.connect("host.example.com", username="deploy", pkey=key, look_for_keys=False)
patterns.note: PKey.from_path sniffs the key type for you. In Paramiko 5 the keyword is password; it was called passphrase in 3.x, so this line breaks silently on upgrade if you passed it by name.

patterns.title: Pin host keys instead of blindly accepting them
patterns.snippet:
import paramiko

client = paramiko.SSHClient()
client.load_host_keys("/etc/myapp/known_hosts")  # writable store
client.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.RejectPolicy())

# AutoAddPolicy() accepts ANY key on first sight and writes it down.
# That is trust-on-first-use with no user prompt: fine for a lab, not for prod.
patterns.note: load_host_keys() marks the file writable so accepted keys are saved; load_system_host_keys() is read-only. Mixing them up means new keys are never persisted.

patterns.title: Transfer files over SFTP
patterns.snippet:
sftp = client.open_sftp()
sftp.put("local/app.tar.gz", "/srv/releases/app.tar.gz")
sftp.get("/var/log/app.log", "local/app.log")
sftp.chmod("/srv/releases/app.tar.gz", 0o640)
sftp.close()
patterns.note: put() will not create missing parent directories and overwrites without warning. Wrap sftp.stat(path) in a try/except IOError to test existence; there is no exists().

patterns.title: List a remote directory with metadata
patterns.snippet:
import stat

sftp = client.open_sftp()
for entry in sftp.listdir_attr("/srv/releases"):
    kind = "dir" if stat.S_ISDIR(entry.st_mode) else "file"
    print(f"{kind}\t{entry.st_size}\t{entry.filename}")
patterns.note: listdir_attr gives you one round trip for names plus stat data; calling listdir() then stat() per file is an extra request each and gets slow over high-latency links.

patterns.title: Stream output line by line instead of buffering
patterns.note: get_pty=True merges stderr into stdout and makes the remote side line-buffer. Without it many programs block-buffer and you see nothing until the process exits.

patterns.title: Reach a private host through a jump box
patterns.snippet:
import paramiko

jump = paramiko.SSHClient()
jump.load_system_host_keys()
jump.connect("bastion.example.com", username="deploy")

channel = jump.get_transport().open_channel(
    "direct-tcpip", dest_addr=("10.0.1.20", 22), src_addr=("127.0.0.1", 0)
)

target = paramiko.SSHClient()
target.load_system_host_keys()
target.connect("10.0.1.20", username="deploy", sock=channel)
patterns.note: This is Paramiko's ProxyJump. Keep the jump client alive for as long as the target connection: closing it kills the channel underneath.

patterns.title: Honour ~/.ssh/config entries
patterns.snippet:
import os, paramiko

cfg = paramiko.SSHConfig.from_path(os.path.expanduser("~/.ssh/config"))
opts = cfg.lookup("myhost")

client = paramiko.SSHClient()
client.load_system_host_keys()
client.connect(
    opts["hostname"],
    port=int(opts.get("port", 22)),
    username=opts.get("user"),
    key_filename=opts.get("identityfile"),
)
patterns.note: Paramiko parses the config but never applies it. Everything (ProxyJump, IdentityFile, Port) must be wired into connect() by hand, which is one of the main reasons people move to Fabric.

patterns.title: Write a key out in OpenSSH format
patterns.snippet:
from paramiko import PKey
from paramiko.pkey import OPENSSH

key = PKey.from_path("/home/me/.ssh/id_rsa", password="old-passphrase")
key.write_private_key_file(
    "/home/me/.ssh/id_rsa_new", password="new-passphrase", file_format=OPENSSH
)
patterns.note: file_format arrived in 5.0.0 and still defaults to legacy PEM; the changelog warns a future major will flip the default, so pass it explicitly now.

patterns.title: Stop long-lived connections from silently dying
patterns.snippet:
client.connect(
    "host.example.com",
    username="deploy",
    timeout=10,        # TCP connect
    banner_timeout=15, # slow SSH banner
    auth_timeout=20,   # slow PAM/LDAP auth
)
client.get_transport().set_keepalive(30)  # seconds
patterns.note: The three timeouts are separate and all default to None or generous values; without keepalive, NAT and load balancers drop idle sessions and the next read hangs instead of raising.

patterns.title: Disable weak or problematic algorithms
patterns.note: This dict is the standard workaround for servers that advertise SHA-2 RSA but reject it. Note that Paramiko 5 already removed SHA-1 kex and ssh-rsa signing, so you cannot re-enable those here.

guide.whatIs: parse-latin is Titus Wormer's natural language tokenizer for Latin-script text. Feed a string to new ParseLatin().parse() and you get an nlcst syntax tree: a RootNode of ParagraphNodes containing SentenceNodes, which hold WordNodes, WhiteSpaceNodes, PunctuationNodes, and SymbolNodes, every node carrying exact line, column, and offset positions. It gets the annoying cases right: periods in e.g. or 1. do not end sentences, and non-profit, she's, G.I., and 11:00 each stay a single word. It is the parser underneath retext-latin, the default parser of the retext ecosystem, which is why a 57-star repo sees close to four million downloads a week.
useIf: You need sentence and word segmentation with exact character offsets, for highlighters, readability scoring, or style checks that must point back into the source string
You are writing or running retext plugins and want the same nlcst tree the rest of the unified ecosystem speaks
Your text mixes Latin-script languages (the README demos French, Icelandic, and Old English) and you want one tokenizer that handles all of them acceptably
You want a small typed dependency: 10.2 KB gzipped, six runtime dependencies all from the same ecosystem, and full TypeScript types
skipIf: You expect linguistics: there is no part-of-speech tagging, lemmatization, entity or sentiment analysis here, only tokenization into a tree; compromise or wink-nlp do actual analysis
Your text is specifically English or Dutch: parse-english and parse-dutch extend this parser with language-specific abbreviation and elision handling and produce better sentence breaks
You just need quick sentence or word splitting and do not care about offsets or tree structure: Intl.Segmenter is built into Node and every modern browser with zero dependencies
You need CJK, Arabic, Hebrew, or other non-Latin scripts: the name is the scope; the README says Cyrillic and Georgian work somewhat, and beyond that quality falls off

You need visible forward motion: no release since 7.0.0 in July 2023, no push since October 2024, and the generated character tables come from Unicode 15.0.0, so characters added to Unicode since then are not classified
guide.setupReality: npm install parse-latin is the easy part; the friction is around it. The package is ESM only, so require() throws in CommonJS and you need dynamic import() or a bundler. The tree is where the learning curve sits: nlcst is a unist-flavored AST, and doing anything useful means adding companions like nlcst-to-string (already one of its six runtime deps), unist-util-visit, and unist-util-inspect, each its own small package. Nothing on the parser is configurable: new ParseLatin().parse(text) is the whole documented API unless you reach into the tokenize plugin arrays. The stated support floor is Node 16, written in 2023 as 'maintained versions of Node', and it has drifted: Node 16 went end-of-life in September 2023 and no new major has followed.

alternatives.name: parse-english
alternatives.when: Your text is English: same tree, plus English abbreviation and elision handling for cleaner sentence breaks

alternatives.name: compromise
alternatives.when: You want part-of-speech tagging, matching, and transformation of English text, not just tokens

alternatives.name: wink-nlp
alternatives.when: You need fast tokenization plus POS, entities, and sentiment in one typed package

guide.verdict: Finished software in the good sense: zero open issues or PRs, a tiny stable API, and it still quietly parses text for the whole retext ecosystem at roughly 3.9M downloads a week. Use it (or parse-english) when you need offset-accurate tokens or live in unified; go elsewhere for actual language understanding.

apiStability.why: One class exposing parse() plus four tokenize methods, unchanged since 7.0.0 shipped in July 2023; earlier majors mostly tracked Node.js support and the nlcst type packages rather than changing behavior.

docsQuality.why: The README documents the full API, spells out the tokenization rules and sentence exceptions, and links a live tree demo; but everything about actually working with the resulting tree lives in separate nlcst and unist docs.

maintenance.why: No release since July 2023 and no push since October 2024, but the tracker sits at zero open issues and PRs, so nothing is being ignored; this reads as done software from the unified maintainer, with the caveat that its generated Unicode tables are pinned at 15.0.0.

ecosystem.why: It is the parser behind retext-latin, retext's default, which is where the roughly 3.9M weekly downloads come from, and every unist utility works on its output; outside unified, effectively nothing consumes nlcst.

patterns.title: Parse a string into an nlcst tree
patterns.note: ESM only: require('parse-latin') throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM in CommonJS; use await import('parse-latin') there. White space containing a line break starts a new ParagraphNode.

patterns.title: Pretty-print the tree while developing
patterns.snippet:
import {ParseLatin} from 'parse-latin'
import {inspect} from 'unist-util-inspect'

console.log(inspect(new ParseLatin().parse('Hi there. Bye.')))
// RootNode[1] (1:1-1:15, 0-14) and so on, indented
patterns.note: unist-util-inspect renders the nested nodes with positions, which beats console.log on a deep tree; the online demo at wooorm.com/parse-latin does the same interactively.

patterns.title: Get a flat token list with tokenize()
patterns.note: tokenize() is the raw first pass: four token categories and no sentence logic. Intra-word merging has not run yet, so she's is still three tokens here; use parse() or tokenizeSentence() to get it as one WordNode.

patterns.title: Parse a fragment at sentence or paragraph level
patterns.note: tokenizeSentence never splits: the whole input becomes one SentenceNode with word merging applied. Splitting on . ! ? happens one level up in tokenizeParagraph, whose plugins also un-split abbreviations like e.g. and 1.

patterns.title: Collect sentence strings from text
patterns.snippet:
import {ParseLatin} from 'parse-latin'
import {toString} from 'nlcst-to-string'
import {visit} from 'unist-util-visit'

const sentences = []
visit(new ParseLatin().parse(text), 'SentenceNode', (node) => {
  sentences.push(toString(node))
})
patterns.note: The reason to use this over splitting on periods is the exception list: e.g., 1., id., initialisms like G.I., and terminal marks inside closing quotes or parens are all handled.

patterns.title: Count words in a document
patterns.note: A word is a run of Unicode letters or numbers plus merged inner marks, so 11:00, N/A, and non-profit each count once; expect the total to differ from text.split on white space.

patterns.title: Turn any node back into text
patterns.snippet:
import {toString} from 'nlcst-to-string'

const firstSentence = tree.children[0].children[0]
toString(firstSentence) // 'One sentence.'
patterns.note: Parent nodes have children, not a value, so there is no text property to read; nlcst-to-string concatenates the leaf values and is already one of parse-latin's own six dependencies.

patterns.title: Map a node back to the source string
patterns.note: Offsets round-trip against the exact input string, which is what makes nlcst usable for linters and highlighters; they stop matching if you trim or normalize the text after parsing.

patterns.title: Use it through retext with plugins
patterns.snippet:
import {retext} from 'retext'
import retextRepeatedWords from 'retext-repeated-words'

const file = await retext()
  .use(retextRepeatedWords)
  .process('It it happens.')
console.error(String(file.messages))
patterns.note: retext's default parser is retext-latin, which is parse-latin underneath, so plugins see exactly the tree described here. When you run plugins, let retext own the parsing instead of instantiating ParseLatin yourself.

patterns.title: Write your own retext plugin over the tree
patterns.note: A retext plugin is just a function returning a transformer that receives the nlcst tree; file.message() reads the node's position automatically, so warnings point at the exact line and column.

patterns.title: Add a custom pass to the tokenizer
patterns.note: The constructor copies the three plugin arrays onto the instance, so mutating parser.tokenizeParagraphPlugins leaves other parsers alone; layering passes like this is exactly how parse-english adds English abbreviation handling.

guide.whatIs: partial-json parses JSON strings that are cut off mid-stream. When an LLM streams a JSON response token by token, JSON.parse fails on every chunk until the very last one; partial-json's parse function instead returns the best complete value it can build from what has arrived so far, so you can render structured data live while it streams. An Allow bitmask controls which types may be incomplete: with STR a half-finished string is returned as-is, without it the parser waits for the closing quote. It is a small pure-JavaScript library with zero dependencies and both CJS and ESM builds.
useIf: You stream JSON from an LLM (tool arguments, structured output) and want to update the UI on every chunk instead of waiting for the final token
You want JSON.parse-compatible behavior on complete input with graceful handling of truncated input, in one function
You need control over what may be partial, for example allow half-open objects but suppress half-finished string values so users never see cut-off text
You need to salvage a value from a response that hit a max-token limit and ended mid-object
skipIf: Your JSON is malformed rather than truncated: partial-json throws on actually invalid input like single quotes or trailing commas, which is jsonrepair territory
You use the Vercel AI SDK or another framework whose streamObject/structured-output helpers already do incremental parsing internally, in which case adding this is redundant
You process multi-megabyte streams where you need incremental event-based parsing: this library reparses the full accumulated string on every call, which is O(n) per chunk and O(n^2) over a stream
You want a battle-hardened core dependency: this is a 0.x package from a small maintainer with sparse commit activity, fine as a UI nicety, riskier as a load-bearing parser
guide.setupReality: npm i partial-json and you are done: zero dependencies, TypeScript types included, works in Node and browsers with both require and import. The things to internalize are behavioral, not install-related. parse defaults to Allow.ALL, which will happily return half-written strings and numbers, so decide your bitmask deliberately. You also still own the streaming loop: accumulate chunks into one string yourself and call parse on each update, and wrap calls in try/catch because a chunk boundary can still leave text the parser considers malformed rather than merely incomplete.

alternatives.name: jsonrepair
alternatives.when: Your input is broken JSON (quotes, commas, comments), not just truncated JSON, and you want it fixed into valid output.

alternatives.name: best-effort-json-parser
alternatives.when: You want maximally forgiving parsing of messy partial JSON without configuring what may be incomplete.

alternatives.name: @streamparser/json
alternatives.when: You need true incremental SAX-style parsing of large JSON streams without reparsing from the start.

guide.verdict: The standard small tool for one specific job: showing structured LLM output while it streams, which explains 5M+ weekly downloads on 243 stars. Use it for that; for repairing invalid JSON or parsing huge streams pick a different tool.

apiStability.why: Still 0.x, but the surface is two exports (parse and Allow) that have not changed in years; there is very little API to break.

docsQuality.why: The README covers the whole API with clear examples and there is a live demo, but that is all the documentation there is; edge-case behavior you learn by experiment.

maintenance.why: Last push June 2026 and only 5 open issues, but it is a small single-org project with an infrequent release cadence; low activity is partly low surface area.

ecosystem.why: Massive incidental reach because AI SDKs and LLM apps pull it in, with a matching Python implementation, but there are no plugins or tooling around it and few third-party resources.

patterns.title: Parse complete JSON like JSON.parse
patterns.note: On complete input parse behaves like JSON.parse, so you can use one code path for both mid-stream and final payloads.

patterns.title: Parse a truncated string with defaults
patterns.note: The default allowance is Allow.ALL, so everything including half-finished strings is returned; pass a bitmask if that is too eager.

patterns.title: Choose which types may be incomplete
patterns.note: Types not in the mask only appear once the parser is sure they are complete; note the unclosed object itself needs OBJ in the mask.

patterns.title: Render streamed LLM JSON incrementally
patterns.note: You accumulate the full string and reparse each time; that is fine for typical LLM response sizes but is quadratic over very long streams.

patterns.title: Suppress half-finished string values in a UI
patterns.note: Useful when showing a cut-off URL or sentence would confuse users; keys and completed values still stream in as they finish.

patterns.title: Import allowance flags without the Allow object
patterns.snippet:
import { parse, STR, OBJ, ARR } from "partial-json";

const result = parse(buffer, STR | OBJ | ARR);
patterns.note: Each Allow property is also a named export; the values are plain numbers combined with bitwise OR.

patterns.title: Handle NaN and Infinity literals
patterns.note: These are not valid JSON, but Python's json.dumps emits them, so the parser accepts them; gate with Allow.SPECIAL if you do not want partial forms.

patterns.title: Distinguish truncated from malformed input
patterns.note: Truncated JSON returns a value; genuinely invalid JSON throws MalformedJSON. Do not use this library expecting repair of bad syntax.

patterns.title: Allow partial literals like tru and nul
patterns.note: With the matching atom flag the parser commits to the only literal the prefix can become; without it the element is omitted until complete.

patterns.title: Use the convenience flag groups
patterns.note: Allow.COLLECTION is the common choice for UIs: structure streams in live while every scalar value waits until it is complete.

guide.whatIs: Passport is Express-compatible authentication middleware for Node.js with exactly one job: authenticate a request, then hand you the result. Everything specific to an identity provider lives in a separate strategy package (the site advertises 500+, covering username/password, OAuth providers, SAML, OpenID Connect, JWT). By design it mounts no routes, stores no users, hashes no passwords, and sends no emails; you write the verify callback, the session serialization, and every screen yourself. The core is three tiny dependencies totalling 2.8 KB gzipped, and it has been frozen since 0.7.0 shipped in November 2023.
useIf: You maintain an Express app that already runs on Passport: the code is stable, the failure modes are documented in a decade of Stack Overflow answers, and ripping out working auth is rarely worth it
You need a niche or legacy identity provider (an old SAML IdP, a regional OAuth provider, CAS) whose only usable Node integration is an existing Passport strategy
You run a classic server-rendered Express app with cookie sessions and want the smallest possible auth hook, wiring storage and hashing yourself on purpose
You are on Nest.js, whose @nestjs/passport wrapper still makes Passport the path of least resistance inside that framework
skipIf: You are starting anything new: the repo has had zero pushes since August 2024 (nearly two years at the time of this review), the only release since 2022 is 0.7.0 from November 2023, 398 issues and PRs sit open, and it is still versioned 0.x after 15 years; treat it as dormant, not merely finished

The strategy ecosystem is dormant too, not just the core: passport-local was last pushed February 2024, passport-jwt February 2024, and passport-google-oauth2 May 2023, and those are the flagship packages, so the long tail is in worse shape

You are outside Express-style middleware (Next.js route handlers, Hono, Fastify idioms, tRPC, edge or serverless runtimes): Passport mutates req and res in ways those runtimes fight, while better-auth and Auth.js were built for them
You expect batteries: no password hashing, no user storage, no CSRF protection, no email verification, no 2FA, no rate limiting; modern alternatives ship all of that and Passport never will
The done(err, user) callback style bothers you: it predates promises, and in an async/await codebase every strategy becomes try/catch glue around a callback
guide.setupReality: npm install passport gets you almost nothing runnable: every auth method is a separate strategy package with its own maintainer and health, and you also need express-session with a real session store (the default MemoryStore leaks and forgets sessions on restart), hand-written serializeUser/deserializeUser, and your own password hashing inside the verify callback. Failure modes are famously silent: wrong middleware order produces redirect loops with no error, and a missing body parser means the strategy never sees credentials. Version drift is the other trap: 0.6.0 (May 2022) made req.logout asynchronous and made login regenerate the session, which broke most tutorials written before then, and since the official docs are thin you will be reading exactly those tutorials.

alternatives.name: better-auth
alternatives.when: New TypeScript project that wants complete auth (email/password, OAuth, 2FA, organizations) from one actively developed framework instead of a middleware kit; note that lucia, the other minimal favourite, is now marked deprecated on npm

alternatives.name: next-auth
alternatives.when: Next.js app; Auth.js works with route handlers and edge runtimes where Passport's middleware model does not fit

alternatives.name: openid-client
alternatives.when: You want certified low-level OAuth 2 / OpenID Connect flows and are comfortable owning sessions and user storage yourself

guide.verdict: Dormant core, enormous installed base: 8.1 million weekly downloads against a repo untouched since August 2024 and flagship strategies that are just as quiet. Keeping it in an existing Express app is defensible; choosing it for anything new in 2026 is not, because the strategy breadth that once justified it now exists in maintained alternatives with far less hand-wiring.

apiStability.why: The API has barely moved in a decade and 0.7.0 changed almost nothing, which is stability of a sort, but the project is still 0.x after 15 years and the 0.6.0 changes (async req.logout, session regeneration on login) broke most published guides in one release.

docsQuality.why: passportjs.org documents happy paths thinly, the session mechanics behind most real bugs (regeneration, serialization, middleware order) are under-explained, and per-strategy docs range from decent to absent, so learning happens through third-party tutorials of mixed vintage, many predating 0.6.0.

maintenance.why: No push to the repo since August 16, 2024, last release November 2023, 398 open issues and PRs, and a largely solo author spread across hundreds of strategy packages; this is dormancy, not stewardship.

ecosystem.why: The advertised 500+ strategies and 8.1M weekly downloads are real assets, but the flagship strategies are themselves stale (passport-local and passport-jwt last pushed February 2024, passport-google-oauth2 May 2023), so the effective ecosystem is smaller and older than the headline number suggests.

patterns.title: Username and password verification
patterns.note: passport-local is a separate package and does zero hashing. done(null, false) means auth failed while done(err) means server error; mixing them up turns bad passwords into 500s.

patterns.title: Store the user in the session
patterns.note: deserializeUser runs on every request that carries a session, so an uncached database lookup here costs one query per page load across your whole app. Serialize only the id, not the whole user object, or stale profile data gets frozen into sessions.

patterns.title: Wire Passport into Express in the right order
patterns.note: Order is everything: body parsing and express-session must both be registered before passport.session(). Get it wrong and you get redirect loops or empty credentials with no error. The default MemoryStore leaks memory, so production needs a real store (connect-redis, connect-mongo).

patterns.title: Authenticate a login POST
patterns.note: If every attempt hits the failure redirect with nothing in the logs, the usual cause is a missing body parser: the strategy never received the credentials at all.

patterns.title: Keep pre-login session data across login (0.6+)
patterns.note: This is the silent 0.6+ behavior change: shopping carts and return-to URLs stored in the session vanish at login unless you pass keepSessionInfo: true. Only enable it when you actually store pre-login state, since it weakens the session fixation defense the regeneration exists for.

patterns.title: Log the user out
patterns.note: req.logout has required a callback since 0.6.0 because it now regenerates the session under the hood; the synchronous req.logout() shown in most older tutorials throws at runtime.

patterns.title: Guard routes behind login
patterns.note: Passport ships no guard middleware; everyone hand-writes this function or pulls in connect-ensure-login, which is itself long unmaintained.

patterns.title: Handle auth results yourself (JSON APIs)
patterns.note: With a custom callback Passport no longer establishes the session for you; forgetting the explicit req.logIn call is the classic silently-logged-out bug. req.logIn also accepts { keepSessionInfo: true } as a second argument if you need pre-login session data.

patterns.title: Stateless API auth with JWT
patterns.note: Pass session: false on token APIs, otherwise Passport still tries to establish a cookie session your API neither has nor wants. passport-jwt itself was last pushed in February 2024, so audit it like any other dormant dependency.

patterns.title: Sign in with Google
patterns.note: callbackURL must match the Google console registration exactly, protocol and port included; mismatches error on Google's consent screen, not in your logs. Use an absolute URL behind proxies or the inferred host will be wrong.

patterns.title: Show why login failed
patterns.note: failureMessage (0.6+) appends to req.session.messages and never clears it, so you must empty the array after rendering or old errors pile up. The older failureFlash option depends on the abandoned connect-flash package.

patterns.title: Accept more than one auth method on a route
patterns.note: Strategies are tried in array order and the first success wins, but every strategy that fails may still write its failure status; the response status comes from the final failure, which surprises people expecting the first.

guide.whatIs: pathspec answers one question well: does this file path match this set of gitignore-style patterns? You compile pattern lines (usually straight out of a .gitignore) into a PathSpec object, then test single paths, filter iterables of paths, or walk a directory tree. It ships two implementations: PathSpec with the 'gitignore' pattern type follows the gitignore documentation literally, while GitIgnoreSpec replicates what Git actually does, including the undocumented edge cases like negations re-including files from excluded directories. It is pure Python with zero required dependencies, and its enormous download count comes from being the ignore engine inside tools like Black and MkDocs.
useIf: Your tool needs to respect .gitignore files the way Git does: GitIgnoreSpec exists precisely for that and matches Git's edge cases, not just the docs
You let users configure include/exclude rules and want them to write familiar gitignore syntax instead of raw regex or fnmatch globs
You need to filter thousands of paths and can install an optional speedup: the backend parameter switches matching to google-re2 or hyperscan for large pattern sets
You want zero required dependencies in a library of your own, since pathspec adds nothing else to your dependency tree
skipIf: You just need simple glob matching on a few paths: fnmatch and pathlib.PurePath.match are in the standard library and cost nothing

You migrated from 0.x without reading the upgrade guide: 1.0 (January 2026) renamed 'gitwildmatch' to 'gitignore' and changed matching behavior for patterns like foo/*, so pinned-then-bumped projects can silently match different files
You need general-purpose advanced globbing (brace expansion, extglob, globstar controls) rather than gitignore semantics: wcmatch covers that ground better
This is a one-person project with a small bus factor; it is steadily maintained but there is no team behind it, which matters if you build a core product feature on its exact matching behavior
guide.setupReality: pip install pathspec is as easy as installs get: pure Python, no compiled parts, Python 3.9+. The gotchas are semantic. You must pick between PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ...) and GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines(...), and the two disagree on real-world patterns; if the goal is 'behave like Git', use GitIgnoreSpec, full stop. Paths are matched as relative strings, so passing absolute paths against patterns written for a repo root quietly matches nothing. Directory patterns need the trailing slash exactly as in gitignore. And if you came from 0.x, 'gitwildmatch' still works but is deprecated with different edge-case behavior than the new 'gitignore' type, which is an easy source of confusing diffs.

alternatives.name: gitignore-parser
alternatives.when: You want a tiny single-purpose parser for one .gitignore file and do not need tree walking or combined specs.

alternatives.name: wcmatch
alternatives.when: You need advanced general globbing (extglob, brace expansion, globstar) beyond gitignore semantics.

guide.verdict: The standard way to do gitignore matching in Python, proven inside Black and MkDocs; use GitIgnoreSpec when fidelity to Git matters. Skip it when stdlib fnmatch would do, and read the 1.0 upgrade notes before bumping from 0.x.

apiStability.why: The core from_lines/match_file surface has been steady for years, but the 1.0 release in January 2026 renamed the main pattern type, deprecated GitWildMatchPattern, and changed matching edge cases, so the 0.x to 1.x jump needs care.

docsQuality.why: The README tutorial and Read the Docs reference cover the API, and the upgrade guide is honest about behavior changes, but explanations of the PathSpec vs GitIgnoreSpec split stay terse and examples are thin.

maintenance.why: Steady releases through 2026 (1.0 in January, 1.1.1 in April), pushed June 2026, and only 8 open issues and PRs; the limiting factor is that it is a single-maintainer project.

ecosystem.why: Around 173M weekly downloads because major tools like Black and MkDocs depend on it, so it is battle-tested everywhere, though there is little plugin ecosystem around such a focused library.

patterns.title: Compile gitignore-style patterns
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', [
    '*.pyc',
    'build/',
    '!build/keep.txt',
])
print(spec.match_file('module.pyc'))  # True
patterns.note: Since 1.0 the pattern type is named 'gitignore'; the old 'gitwildmatch' name still works but is deprecated and keeps slightly different edge-case behavior.

patterns.title: Load patterns from a .gitignore file
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import GitIgnoreSpec

with open('.gitignore') as fh:
    spec = GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines(fh)

print(spec.match_file('dist/app.tar.gz'))
patterns.note: from_lines accepts any iterable of lines, so the open file object can be passed directly; comments and blank lines are handled like Git does.

patterns.title: Match exactly like Git, edge cases included
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import GitIgnoreSpec

spec = GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines([
    'logs/',
    '!logs/important.log',
])
print(spec.match_file('logs/debug.log'))      # True
print(spec.match_file('logs/important.log'))  # False (re-included)
patterns.note: GitIgnoreSpec replicates Git's real behavior, including negations inside excluded directories, where plain PathSpec follows the documentation instead.

patterns.title: Check one path
patterns.snippet:
from pathlib import PurePath
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ['docs/**/*.md'])
spec.match_file('docs/guide/intro.md')      # True
spec.match_file(PurePath('docs/README.md')) # pathlib works too
patterns.note: Paths are matched as given, relative to the implied root of the patterns; absolute paths against repo-relative patterns will not match.

patterns.title: Filter an existing list of paths
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ['*.tmp', 'cache/'])
files = ['a.txt', 'b.tmp', 'cache/x.json']
ignored = set(spec.match_files(files))
kept = [f for f in files if f not in ignored]
patterns.note: match_files returns a generator of the matching (ignored) entries; wrap it in set or list before reusing it.

patterns.title: Walk a directory tree for matches
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ['**/*.log'])
for rel_path in spec.match_tree_files('/var/app'):
    print(rel_path)
patterns.note: Yields paths relative to the root you pass in, walking the filesystem for you; use match_files instead if you already have the path list.

patterns.title: Invert matching to select files to keep
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import GitIgnoreSpec

spec = GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines(open('.gitignore'))
keep = set(spec.match_tree_files('project/', negate=True))
patterns.note: Specs positively match the ignored files by default; negate=True flips the result, which is what backup and packaging tools usually want.

patterns.title: Combine multiple pattern sources
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

base = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', open('.gitignore'))
local = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', open('.gitignore.local'))
spec = base + local  # later patterns win, like nested .gitignore files
patterns.note: The + operator concatenates pattern lists, preserving order, so later negations can re-include files excluded by earlier specs.

patterns.title: Speed up matching with an alternate regex backend
patterns.snippet:
# pip install 'pathspec[re2]'
from pathspec import GitIgnoreSpec

spec = GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines(lines, backend='re2')
# or backend='hyperscan', or the default backend='best'
patterns.note: New in 1.0. The default 'best' picks the fastest installed backend; re2 tends to win at high pattern counts per the project's own benchmarks.

patterns.title: Find out which pattern matched
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ['*.log', '!keep.log'])
result = spec.check_file('debug.log')
print(result.include)  # True if ignored
print(result.index)    # index of the deciding pattern
patterns.note: check_file returns a result object instead of a bare bool, which is what you need for 'why is this file ignored' debugging output.

guide.whatIs: pdfminer.six reads the text out of PDF files by interpreting the drawing instructions inside them, not by looking at pictures of pages. It walks the content stream, decodes the fonts and character maps, and reports every glyph with its exact position on the page, then runs a layout pass that groups those glyphs into words, lines, and text boxes. You can take the one-line answer (extract_text gives you a string) or take the layout tree and decide yourself what counts as a paragraph, a column, or a table cell, using coordinates and font names. It is a community-maintained fork of the original PDFMiner, written entirely in Python, and it is the engine underneath pdfplumber and a lot of document-processing pipelines.
useIf: You need text plus geometry: every character comes with a bounding box, a font name, and a size, which is what you build invoice and form parsers on
You want to write your own grouping logic rather than accept someone's paragraph heuristics, because extract_pages hands you the raw LTPage tree
Your PDFs are encrypted with a password (RC4 or AES) or contain CJK and vertical writing, both of which are handled without extra packages
You need something that installs into a slim container or a lambda without system PDF libraries, and a pdf2txt.py command line that works immediately
skipIf: Your PDFs are scans: pdfminer only reads text drawing operators, so a page of images returns an empty string with no warning and no error. You need OCR first (ocrmypdf or pytesseract), and nothing in the library will tell you that is the problem
You need tables as rows and columns: you get characters and boxes with coordinates and nothing table-shaped, which is exactly why pdfplumber and camelot exist on top of it
Throughput matters: it is pure Python doing per-glyph work, so batch extraction over thousands of documents is far slower than pypdfium2 or PyMuPDF, which wrap a C or C++ engine
You want to write PDFs: this library only reads. Merging, splitting, rotating, watermarking, or filling forms all need pypdf or something else
You need HTML, XML, or hOCR output you can trust: those output types exist, but the library's own docstring for extract_text_to_fp says only 'text' works properly

You need bugs fixed on a schedule: the README states plainly that maintainer availability is limited and that submitting a pull request yourself is the best way to get an issue resolved, and 213 issues (223 counting PRs) are open
guide.setupReality: pip install pdfminer.six on Python 3.10 or newer. The library itself is pure Python, but it pulls cryptography for RC4 and AES decryption and charset-normalizer for encodings, and cryptography is a compiled wheel, so an unusual platform without a prebuilt wheel drags in a Rust toolchain. Image extraction is an extra: pip install 'pdfminer.six[image]' adds Pillow. Two naming traps catch people. The distribution is pdfminer.six with a dot but the import is plain pdfminer, and the abandoned original pdfminer package is still sitting on PyPI, so installing the wrong name gives you dead code from years ago. The console scripts keep their suffix too, so the commands are literally pdf2txt.py and dumppdf.py. Versions are dates like 20260107 rather than semver, which means pinning is exact-match and a release number tells you nothing about whether it breaks you; read the changelog instead. The real configuration cost is LAParams, whose defaults (char_margin 2.0, line_margin 0.5, word_margin 0.1, boxes_flow 0.5) decide where paragraphs and columns land, and getting sensible output on your own documents almost always means tuning them.

alternatives.name: pdfplumber
alternatives.when: You want tables, word-level extraction, cropping, and page images without writing layout code; it wraps this exact library and pins pdfminer.six==20260107.

alternatives.name: pypdfium2
alternatives.when: You need speed or page rendering to images and want permissive licensing, since it binds Google's pdfium under BSD and Apache terms.

alternatives.name: pymupdf
alternatives.when: You want the fastest and most complete extraction available and your project can accept AGPL, or you are willing to buy the commercial license.

alternatives.name: pypdf
alternatives.when: Your job is manipulating files (merge, split, rotate, encrypt) with rough text extraction on the side, and you want a pure-Python package with light dependencies.

guide.verdict: The dependable pure-Python way to get text with exact coordinates out of digital PDFs, and the foundation the nicer libraries are built on. It is slow, it does nothing for scanned pages, and it will never hand you a table, so choose it when you want control over layout data rather than a finished answer.

apiStability.why: extract_text, extract_pages, and the LAParams and converter classes have kept the same signatures for years, and date-stamped releases are fixes rather than redesigns; the 20251230 security release did force anyone with custom pickled CMaps to convert them to JSON.

docsQuality.why: pdfminersix.readthedocs.io has task-shaped tutorials (text, images, form data), a topics section that actually explains the coordinate system and every LAParams knob, and generated API pages; the converter classes stay thin and the non-text output modes are barely covered.

maintenance.why: Last pushed March 2026 with 213 open issues (223 counting PRs) and a README that says maintainer availability is limited and PRs are the fastest route to a fix; security work does still land, such as CVE-2025-64512 replacing pickled CMap storage with JSON in the 20251230 release.

ecosystem.why: Around 16.9 million weekly downloads and 7,015 stars, and it is the layer other tools sit on: pdfplumber depends on it directly with an exact pin, so answers and worked examples for coordinate-level PDF work almost always assume it.

patterns.title: Get the whole document as a string
patterns.snippet:
from pdfminer.high_level import extract_text

text = extract_text("example.pdf")
print(text)
patterns.note: Accepts a path or an already-open binary file object. An empty or nearly empty result almost always means the pages are scanned images, not that the file is broken.

patterns.title: Read only the pages you need
patterns.snippet:
from pdfminer.high_level import extract_text

first_two = extract_text("report.pdf", page_numbers=[0, 1])
cover = extract_text("report.pdf", maxpages=1)
patterns.note: page_numbers is zero-indexed, so page 1 of the document is 0. Passing a set instead of a list is faster on long documents because membership is checked once per page.

patterns.title: Fix wrong paragraph and column grouping
patterns.snippet:
from pdfminer.high_level import extract_text
from pdfminer.layout import LAParams

params = LAParams(line_margin=0.3, char_margin=1.5, boxes_flow=0.5)
text = extract_text("two-column.pdf", laparams=params)

# read strictly in position order, no grouping heuristics:
raw = extract_text("odd.pdf", laparams=LAParams(boxes_flow=None))
patterns.note: All the margins are relative to character or line size, not absolute points. boxes_flow runs from -1.0 (horizontal position only) to +1.0 (vertical only); setting it to None turns off advanced ordering entirely, which is often what you want for a fixed template.

patterns.title: Walk the layout tree instead of taking a string
patterns.note: extract_pages is a generator, so pages are parsed lazily and memory stays flat. Coordinates start at the bottom-left of the page in PDF points (72 per inch), so y grows upward, the opposite of screen coordinates.

patterns.title: Read font name and size per character
patterns.note: A text line also contains LTAnno objects for spaces and newlines that the layout pass inserted; those have no font or position, which is why the isinstance check on LTChar matters. Font names arrive with the PDF subset prefix, as in ABCDEF+Helvetica.

patterns.title: Pull a value from a fixed spot on the page
patterns.note: Check page.mediabox before hardcoding numbers, since A4 and Letter differ and a rotated page swaps width and height. This is how template-based invoice parsing gets built on pdfminer.

patterns.title: Open a password-protected PDF
patterns.snippet:
from pdfminer.high_level import extract_text

text = extract_text("protected.pdf", password="hunter2")
patterns.note: This handles user passwords on RC4 and AES encrypted files. An owner-password-only file (no password needed to open, but copying is disallowed) still extracts, because pdfminer reads the content rather than honoring the permission flag.

patterns.title: Save embedded images to disk
patterns.note: Images usually sit inside an LTFigure rather than at the top level of the page, which is why the nested loop is needed. export_image returns the filename it chose and picks the extension from the image encoding, so you may get .jpg, .png, or a raw .bmp.

patterns.title: Read document metadata and the table of contents
patterns.note: Values in doc.info come back as raw bytes, so decode them yourself and expect encoding surprises. get_outlines raises PDFNoOutlines rather than yielding nothing when the document has no bookmarks.

patterns.title: Tell a scanned PDF from a digital one before you parse it
patterns.note: There is no built-in flag for this, and no exception is raised, so a scan silently produces empty output. Sampling the first few pages keeps the check cheap on long documents.

patterns.title: Extract from the command line
patterns.snippet:
pdf2txt.py example.pdf > out.txt
pdf2txt.py -p 1,2 -o out.txt example.pdf
pdf2txt.py -P hunter2 protected.pdf

# inspect the PDF object structure
dumppdf.py -a example.pdf | head -40
patterns.note: The .py suffix is part of the installed command name, which trips up anyone typing pdf2txt. dumppdf.py is the tool to reach for when extraction returns nothing and you need to see what objects the file actually contains.

patterns.title: Write output through the low-level entry point
patterns.snippet:
from io import StringIO
from pdfminer.high_level import extract_text_to_fp
from pdfminer.layout import LAParams

with open("example.pdf", "rb") as fin:
    out = StringIO()
    extract_text_to_fp(fin, out, laparams=LAParams(), output_type="text")
    print(out.getvalue())
patterns.note: This is what pdf2txt.py calls, and it takes options extract_text does not, including rotation, scale, and output_dir for images. Note that omitting laparams here is not the same as passing LAParams(): None skips layout analysis entirely.

guide.whatIs: pdfplumber reads a machine-generated PDF and hands you its raw geometry: every character with its font, size, and bounding box, plus every line, rectangle, curve, image, and annotation on the page. On top of that primitive layer it adds the two things people actually come for. First, a text extractor that can approximate the visual layout instead of flattening everything into one string. Second, a table finder that rebuilds a cell grid from the page's ruling lines, or from word alignment when the table has no lines at all. It can also render any page to a PNG and draw the detected edges and cells on top, which turns table debugging from guesswork into looking at a picture. It is built on pdfminer.six and inherits that library's parsing accuracy along with its speed.
useIf: You need coordinates and not just text: pulling the value that sits to the right of a label, or reading a fixed region of a form, is a crop plus an extract_text call
You extract tables from digital PDFs that have visible ruling lines and you want a row-by-cell grid rather than a text blob
